claim: getlocalhost.app ('localhost app') is a free, MIT-licensed open-source desktop process manager for local development that starts/stops/watches dev servers, workers and databases from one window; positioned as a GUI alternative to pm2/foreman/tmux.
quote: localhost app (getlocalhost.app) is a free, open-source desktop process manager for local development: it starts, stops and watches all your dev servers, workers and databases from one window instead of terminal tabs.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Platform support: macOS 15+ (Apple silicon or Intel, native SwiftUI), Windows 10/11 x64, and Linux (.deb Ubuntu 22.04+/Debian 12+, .rpm Fedora, AppImage, x86_64); Windows/Linux builds are Tauri over a shared Rust core.
quote: SwiftUI on macOS, one light app for Linux and Windows, all on one Rust core.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Pricing model: completely free, MIT open source, no account, no backend, works offline.
quote: Yes. localhost is free and open source under the MIT license. There is no account and no backend, and it works offline.
location: FAQ 'Is it free and open source?'
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Core data model: a Project is a folder; a Service is one long-running command in it (e.g. pnpm dev, docker compose up postgres, cargo run); a Port is how a Service is known to be Running.
quote: A Project is a folder; a Service is one long-running command in it, such as `pnpm dev`, `uv run fastapi dev` or `docker compose up postgres`. localhost runs it in your login shell, keeps its output, knows when it is up, and stops its whole process tree when you ask.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Service auto-detection scans the project folder and suggests Services from package.json scripts (with default ports for known dev servers passed as $PORT), Docker Compose files (one 'Infra' service or per-service), Python apps (Django/FastAPI/Flask via uv/Poetry/Pipenv/venv), and Cargo binaries; every suggestion must be manually checked before saving.
quote: **Node**: `package.json` scripts, run with your package manager (`pnpm run dev`, …). Known dev servers get their default port, passed as `$PORT`. **Docker Compose**: one `Infra` Service running the whole file (`docker compose up`, in the foreground), or one per Compose service (`docker compose up <service>`) if you’d rather. **Python**: Django, FastAPI and Flask apps, with uv, Poetry, Pipenv or a virtualenv. **Cargo**: `cargo run` for each binary.
title: Quick start

claim: Commands run in the user's login shell ($SHELL -l -c) so PATH/version managers/profiles apply; on Windows they run in cmd.exe with the user environment read fresh at every start.
quote: one command line, run in your login shell (`$SHELL -l -c "…"`), so your `PATH`, version managers and profile apply. Pipes, `&&` and `$VARIABLES` work as in a terminal. On Windows itself it runs in `cmd.exe`.
title: Services and states

claim: A Service counts as Running once its configured Port accepts TCP connections (30s timeout → Running anyway with a warning); without a Port it is Running after ~1.5 seconds alive.
quote: With a Port, a Service counts as Running once the port accepts connections. After 30 seconds it is Running anyway, with a warning that clears when the port opens. Without a Port, it is Running after about 1.5 seconds alive.
title: Ports

claim: Port-conflict handling: before start it checks who holds the port; the Service can auto-start on the next free port for that Run only (config unchanged), or user chooses kill-holder/another-port/cancel; dependents and same-project holders never get moved.
quote: Before starting a Service with a Port, localhost checks who holds it. If something else does, the Service can start on the next free port (it gets that port as `$PORT` for this Run; the configured Port doesn’t change), or you choose: stop the other process and start, start on another port, or cancel.
title: Ports

claim: Ports view lists every TCP listener on the machine attributed to: a managed Service, a process inside a Project folder, or unmanaged (system/other apps folded below); user can stop listeners from the view (confirmation for foreign processes).
quote: The **Ports** view (**⌘0**) lists every process listening on a TCP port and whom it belongs to: one of your Services, a process running inside one of your Projects’ folders, or nothing localhost knows (other apps and system services are folded below). Select one and press ⌘. to stop it; localhost asks first for anything it didn’t start.
title: Ports

claim: Env handling: layered variables — login shell env < Project vars < Service vars < active Environment Profile (per-project profiles like Development/Testing); PORT plus FORCE_COLOR/CLICOLOR_FORCE/PYTHONUNBUFFERED injected; changes need restart ('Restart to apply').
quote: 1. your login shell’s environment (on Windows, your user environment as a new sign-in would see it), 2. the Project’s variables, 3. the Service’s variables, 4. the active Environment Profile’s variables (picked in the Project’s toolbar), plus `PORT` when it has a Port, and `FORCE_COLOR=1`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`
title: Environment and Secrets

claim: Secrets: any variable can be locked into the OS secret store — macOS login Keychain, Linux Secret Service (GNOME Keyring/KWallet/KeePassXC), Windows Credential Manager; secret values never written to config files, logs or Project files.
quote: its value goes to your system’s secret store and stays hidden until you click the eye. Secret values are never written to configuration files, logs or Project files.
title: Environment and Secrets

claim: Services have six states: Stopped, Starting, Running, Stopping, Exited (exit code 0), Failed (with reason + last output shown).
quote: A Service is always in one of six states: Stopped | Starting | Running | Stopping | Exited | Failed
title: Services and states

claim: Stop semantics: SIGINT (Ctrl-C) to the whole process group, SIGTERM after 5s, then SIGKILL; on Windows Ctrl-Break then kill every started process — 'nothing is left running in the background'.
quote: Stopping sends Ctrl-C (SIGINT) to the Service’s whole process group, then SIGTERM after 5 seconds, then SIGKILL, so nothing is left running in the background. On Windows itself it sends Ctrl-Break, then ends every process the Service started.
title: Services and states

claim: Deliberately NO auto-restart/crash-loop backoff: 'It never restarts a Service on its own' — diverges from Dev Dashboard's backoff+circuit-breaker model; positioning is dev servers, not production keep-alive (pm2's job).
quote: It never restarts a Service on its own. To keep processes running in production, keep pm2.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Dependencies: 'Starts after' per Service; Start All runs in dependency order, Stop All in reverse; stopping a service leaves dependents alone; failed dependency blocks waiters. Optional 'Run before' pre-command and 'Manual' flag (Start All skips it).
quote: Starting a Service starts its Dependencies first. **Start All** goes in dependency order, **Stop All** in reverse. Stopping or restarting one Service leaves the Services that depend on it alone. If a Dependency fails, the Services waiting for it don’t start, and say why.
title: Services and states

claim: MCP server 'localhost mcp' exposes 15 tools (9 run/inspect: list_projects, list_services, status, start_service, stop_service, start_project, stop_project, logs, ports; 6 edit: create/update/delete project+service) sharing one background core with the app; status reports startedBy: app|agent.
quote: Fifteen tools: nine to run and inspect, six to add, edit and remove.
location: Which MCP tools does localhost expose?
title: localhost app’s MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex

claim: Agent-started services stop when the agent disconnects unless the app is open (then they keep running); never starts a second copy of a running service; --read-only mode strips editing tools; destructive ops need confirm:true and never touch the project folder.
quote: When the agent disconnects, the Services it started stop, unless the app is open: then they keep running there, until you stop them.
location: How does localhost app fix it?
title: localhost app’s MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex

claim: Machines: add a remote computer reachable via existing ssh (keys, ~/.ssh/config, ProxyJump, Tailscale); runs 'ssh <dest> localhost remote --stdio' — remote Projects appear in the sidebar and are fully controllable; Open in Browser forwards the remote port to the same local port via SSH; config/secrets stay on the remote.
quote: localhost reaches it with your system’s `ssh`, as you already do from a terminal. Its Projects show in the sidebar below this computer’s, and you add, edit, start, stop and watch them from here.
title: Run dev servers on another computer over SSH

claim: Machine reconnect uses escalating backoff 1s→2s→5s→15s→30s; a connection is counted dead after 45s silence; remote-started-from-here services stop on disconnect unless the app is open there.
quote: A lost connection is made again on its own, after 1 second, then 2, 5, 15, and every 30 seconds, and its Projects and statuses are read again.
title: Run dev servers on another computer over SSH

claim: Windows specifics: per-user install (no admin), Execution Target per project = Windows or a WSL 2 distro; for WSL it copies a 'localhostd' helper into the distro; MCP shares the core via an ACL'd named pipe \\.\pipe\localhostd-<n>; fnm/mise-activate version managers unseen, shims/nvm-windows/Volta seen.
quote: the app and the agent share one background core, reached through a named pipe (`\\.\pipe\localhostd-<number>`) that only your user can open.
title: Windows and WSL

claim: Update model: checks GitHub Releases at launch + every 6h (only network call); notice → background download → 'Restart to Update' which stops running services first after asking; updates signed, verified against a key built into the app; .deb/.rpm update via package manager; macOS self-updates even when brew-installed; auto-check can be disabled.
quote: localhost checks GitHub Releases for a new version at launch and then every 6 hours. It offers a new version; it never installs one without asking.
title: How localhost updates on macOS, Windows, Linux

claim: Releases are currently unsigned by a known publisher: macOS not notarized (Open Anyway / xattr quarantine workaround), Windows SmartScreen 'More info → Run anyway' once.
quote: Releases aren’t notarized or signed by a known publisher yet, so macOS and Windows ask once at first launch.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: Local-first storage: no account/backend; configuration lives in localhost's own storage, nothing written into the repo; a Project can be exported as a shareable Project file.
quote: Configuration lives in localhost’s own storage. Export a Project file when you want to share one.
title: localhost app: desktop process manager for local dev servers

claim: UI structure: sidebar of Projects (+Machines below), Services column, Ports view (⌘0), 'All services' merged log with per-service Key prefix, command palette, menu-bar/tray icon with red-dot Failed badge, welcome dialog + 'Get started' checklist onboarding. Closing the window keeps services running; quitting stops them (asks first).
quote: Select **All services** to see every Service’s output in one stream, each line prefixed with its Key. ... Closing the window doesn’t stop anything: your Services keep running, and the menu bar icon (the tray icon on Linux and Windows) shows them, with a red dot while one has Failed. Quitting asks first, then stops everything.
title: Quick start

claim: Python env detection: nearest .venv/venv/virtualenv in working dir or above (up to project root) auto-attached as Service's Python environment ('Using detected .venv'), PATH+VIRTUAL_ENV set without rewriting the command; skipped for uv run/poetry run/pipenv run commands.
quote: localhost fills it in with the nearest `.venv`, `venv` or `virtualenv` in the working directory or a folder above it, up to the Project’s, and says so in the editor: “Using detected .venv”. It doesn’t for commands that already pick their environment (`uv run`, `poetry run`, `pipenv run`, `.venv/bin/uvicorn`), and scanning again never changes existing Services
title: Services and states

claim: Crash recovery: if the background core crashes, next launch detects services still running from it and asks whether to stop them (re-attach model).
quote: If localhost’s background core ever crashes, the next launch finds the Services still running from it and asks whether to stop them.
title: Services and states
